screens.title: Updating and Deleting Documents
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a dependable habit for changing and removing data in MongoDB. We cover how to target documents with filters, update fields with operators such as set, increment, unset and array modifiers, and when to use a full replace versus a targeted update. You will also practice safe deletion patterns and how to verify results so you avoid accidental data loss. Throughout we use concrete shell examples and a short customers lab that illustrates common tasks: change an email, bump a counter, add an array tag, revive inactive customers and remove a single record. Why this matters: update and delete operations are destructive when done incorrectly, so learning to verify filters and check operation results is essential to being a responsible DBA. Expect short live-coding demonstrations and reflection prompts that help you decide when a replace is appropriate versus a targeted update. At the end you’ll be able to pick the right method, run it safely, and confirm the change.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Updating & Deleting Documents
Updating & Deleting Documents
Learn operators, replacements, and safe deletion patterns
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

updateOne/updateMany, replaceOne, deleteOne/deleteMany, operators and verification.

Why it matters

A single wrong filter or missing operator can replace or remove many documents.

Focus areas

Filter creation, operator usage, result inspection, safety checks.

Hands-on

Filter
Query that selects documents by criteria, e.g., name or status.
Update Doc
Contains operators like set, inc, unset, push that modify fields.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will be able to perform targeted updates and deletions with confidence. First, you will use updateOne and updateMany to change single or multiple documents, creating precise filter documents that limit the scope of change. Second, you will apply and combine update operators such as set to change values, inc to increment counters, unset to remove fields, and push or pull to modify arrays. Third, you will recognize when replaceOne is appropriate for a full-document replacement and how it differs from an operator-based update. Finally, you will perform deletion operations with deleteOne and deleteMany while applying safety checks to avoid mass data loss. Each objective includes a short practice task so you can verify the results using the returned counts and acknowledged flags. These skills matter because updates and deletes are destructive when misused; we focus on filters, verification, and safe workflows to keep your data accurate and intact.

screens.title: updateOne() and updateMany() — filter + update document
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the fundamental shape of an update operation. Every update call has two primary parts: a filter document and an update document. The filter is a query that selects which documents will be considered. If you use updateOne, at most a single matching document changes. If you use updateMany, all documents that match that filter are modified. The update document normally uses special update operators such as set or inc; without any update operator MongoDB treats the second argument as a full replacement. A concrete example: to change a product price you build a filter for the product identity and an update document with set to alter the price. A common misconception is assuming updateOne updates one field only — updateOne will apply whatever operators you supply to one matching document, including adding or removing several fields at once. Another pitfall is an overly permissive filter; an empty filter or a filter with broad criteria can update many records unexpectedly. Key takeaway: always design a precise filter and prefer operator-based updates for partial changes. Which fields will you include in your filter next time you update data?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: updateOne updates a single matching document; updateMany updates all matches. Both take a filter and an update document that usually contains update operators.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › updateOne / updateMany
What they are

Both methods accept a filter and an update document. updateOne changes at most one document; updateMany changes every match. Use precise filters and operator-based update documents to avoid accidental replacement.

Example
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Laptop Pro X" },
  { $set: { price: 1399.99, lastUpdated: new Date() } }
)
Common mistake
Omitting update operators causes a full document replacement, which can remove fields unintentionally.
Check
Run find() with the same filter before updating to see what will change.
Explanation and walk-through
  • Filter identifies candidate documents; choose fields that uniquely match your target.
  • Update document with operators modifies only the specified fields so the rest remains intact.
  • updateOne applies to one matched document even if more match; updateMany affects all matches.
Key takeaway
Design precise filters and use update operators to change only what you intend.

screens.title: $set for single and multiple field updates
screens.narratorSegment: The $set operator is the most common tool for changing values inside a document. It assigns a field to a new value and creates the field when it doesn't exist. Use $set when you need to change single fields like an email or multiple fields such as price and lastUpdated in one command. A concrete example is updating a customer's email: you build a filter that matches the customer's name and a $set update specifying the new email address. A typical misconception is using $set when you actually want to remove a field; for removals use $unset. Another important detail: $set only touches listed fields, leaving everything else intact, which makes it safe for partial updates. After running $set, check the command result for modifiedCount to confirm the change. Practice: preview with find(), then run an updateOne that uses $set to change two fields, and verify modifiedCount equals one. This habit makes partial updates predictable and reversible through controlled changes or backups. $set for single and multiple field updates means $set changes or adds specified fields. combine multiple assignments in one update document to change several fields atomically on the matched document.. In practical terms, set a field value or multiple fields safely with $set. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: $set
keyIdea.text: $set changes or adds specified fields. Combine multiple assignments in one update document to change several fields atomically on the matched document.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Using $set
Command demo
// Update single field (email)
db.customers.updateOne(
  { firstName: "Alice", lastName: "Smith" },
  { $set: { email: "alice.s@newdomain.com" } }
)

// Update multiple fields
 db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Laptop Pro X" },
  { $set: { price: 1399.99, lastUpdated: new Date() } }
)
Run find() with the same filter before executing to confirm the target document. After the update, inspect the result.modifiedCount to confirm the operation modified the expected number of documents.
Explanation & tips
  • $set will only modify the fields you list; do not rely on it to remove fields.
  • You can set nested fields using dot notation; this will create intermediate objects if needed.
  • Combine multiple $set assignments in a single update document to make changes atomically for that operation.
Key Takeaway

$set is the safe default for partial updates; preview with find() and use modifiedCount to verify.

screens.title: $inc and $unset — counters and field removal
screens.narratorSegment: $inc and $unset are complementary operators you will use frequently. Use $inc to increment or decrement a numeric field by a specified amount. It creates the field if it doesn't exist and applies the numeric change. For example, incrementing an orderCount by one is a standard operation for tracking activity. One misconception is expecting $inc to create non-numeric fields; if the target field has a non-numeric value the operation will fail. Use $unset when you want to remove a field entirely from a document. The value you supply to $unset is ignored; the presence of the field key in $unset signals removal. A common error is attempting to set a field to null to remove it — null leaves an empty field, while $unset removes the key. In practice, combine these operators where appropriate: increment counters for analytics and unset deprecated fields that no longer serve the document model. After each operation, confirm the modifiedCount to ensure the intended documents changed. $inc and $unset — counters and field removal means $inc changes numeric fields by an amount and $unset removes a field key from matching documents.. In practical terms, increment numeric fields and remove unwanted fields safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operators
keyIdea.text: $inc changes numeric fields by an amount and $unset removes a field key from matching documents.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › $inc & $unset
$inc example
// Increment a counter
 db.customers.updateOne(
  { firstName: "Charlie", lastName: "Brown" },
  { $inc: { orderCount: 1 } }
)
If orderCount does not exist, $inc will create it with the increment amount. Ensure the existing field is numeric or the operation will fail.
$unset example
// Remove a field
 db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Wireless Mouse" },
  { $unset: { tags: "" } }
)
The value given to $unset is ignored; the operator removes the field key entirely. Use $unset when you want to clean up deprecated fields.
Pro tip

When migrating schemas, sequence updates to add new fields before you unset old ones to avoid losing data prematurely.

screens.title: $push and $pull — modifying arrays
screens.narratorSegment: Arrays are common in MongoDB documents and the $push and $pull operators let you manage them directly. Use $push to append a value to an array field. If the field does not exist, MongoDB will create an array containing the pushed value. $pull removes all instances of a specified value from an array. A frequent use is adding tags or status markers and later removing specific ones. A misconception is treating $push like a set — it does not prevent duplicates; repeated pushes create repeated elements. To avoid duplicates, you can use $addToSet (not covered in detail here) or check presence before pushing. Think through your application semantics: do you want multiple identical entries or a unique list? Additionally, applying these operators inside updateMany modifies every matching document's arrays; verify with find() first. Example tasks: push a VIP tag into a user's orders array, then pull it out to simulate removing that tag. After each operation, inspect the document to confirm the array content and length. $push and $pull — modifying arrays means $push appends values to arrays, creating the array if absent; $pull removes all matching values from an array.. In practical terms, append and remove values from array fields safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › $push / $pull
$push example
 db.customers.updateOne(
  { firstName: "Diana", lastName: "Prince" },
  { $push: { orders: "VIP" } }
)
If orders isn't an array, the field becomes an array with the new value. $push does not enforce uniqueness.
$pull example
 db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Laptop Pro X" },
  { $pull: { tags: "premium" } }
)
$pull removes all array elements equal to the supplied value. If none match, the document remains unchanged and modifiedCount is zero.
Common mistake

Pushing without checking for duplicates can bloat arrays. Pulling with a broad criterion may remove multiple expected values; preview with find() first.

screens.title: replaceOne() — when to replace the whole document
screens.narratorSegment: replaceOne substitutes an entire document for the first match of the filter, preserving only the existing _id value. Because it replaces, not updates, any fields left out of the replacement document will be removed. Use replaceOne when you want to provide a complete, new document shape — for example, a canonical record produced by a migration or a strict replacement after validation. A common misconception is believing replaceOne is just a different name for updateOne; it's not. If you omit update operators in an update call, MongoDB may treat the call as a replacement and replace the document. To avoid accidental replacement, always use operators when you intend partial changes. In practice, before using replaceOne, run a find() to capture the existing document for backup, and be explicit about fields you want to keep. The key decision: choose replaceOne when you intentionally want to control the entire document contents; otherwise prefer operator-based updates for minimal, safer changes. replaceOne() — when to replace the whole document means use replaceone to replace a full document. missing fields in the replacement are removed, so prefer it only when you intend a complete substitution.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: replaceOne
keyIdea.text: Use replaceOne to replace a full document. Missing fields in the replacement are removed, so prefer it only when you intend a complete substitution.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › replaceOne
Replace example
 db.products.replaceOne(
  { name: "Wireless Mouse" },
  { name: "Ergonomic Wireless Mouse", category: "Accessories", price: 60.00, inStock: true }
 )
This replacement will remove any fields that existed previously but are not listed here, except for _id which is preserved.
Best practices
  • Backup or capture the existing document with find() before replacing.
  • Include every field you want to keep, or migrate fields intentionally.
  • Prefer operator updates for partial changes to avoid accidental data loss.
Safety note

A mistaken replace operation can remove fields permanently. Use with care and verify the replacement document fully.

screens.title: deleteOne() and deleteMany() — removal with extreme care
screens.narratorSegment: Deleting documents is irreversible in normal operation, so we treat delete commands with high caution. deleteOne removes a single document that matches the filter; deleteMany removes every document that matches. A dangerous mistake is passing an empty filter to deleteMany, which will remove the entire collection. Best practice: always run find() with the same filter first, review the result set, and then run the delete operation. Use deleteOne when you intend to remove a single known record like a user by unique name or identifier. Use deleteMany for bulk cleanups but only after validating the filter. After the operation, inspect the returned deletedCount to confirm how many documents were removed. If the count is larger than expected, you must restore from backups or point-in-time snapshots. The habit of previewing and verifying reduces the likelihood of catastrophic data loss and makes deletion operations predictable and auditable. deleteOne() and deleteMany() — removal with extreme care means deleteone deletes a single matching document. deletemany deletes all matches; preview filters first to avoid accidental mass deletion.. In practical terms, selectively remove one or many documents and avoid catastrophic filters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deletes
keyIdea.text: deleteOne deletes a single matching document. deleteMany deletes all matches; preview filters first to avoid accidental mass deletion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › deleteOne / deleteMany
Examples
// Delete a single customer
 db.customers.deleteOne({ firstName: "Eve", lastName: "Adams" })

// Delete all out-of-stock products
 db.products.deleteMany({ inStock: false })
Always preview the filter with find() to confirm the documents that will be removed. After deletion, check deletedCount for the number removed.
Safety checklist
  • Run find() with the filter before deleting.
  • Avoid deleteMany({}) without a restrictive filter.
  • Confirm deletedCount and keep backups or snapshots available.
Warning

An empty filter to deleteMany will match all documents and empty the collection.

screens.title: Customers lab — step-by-step shell walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: We will walk through the customers lab step-by-step so you experience each operator in context. Start by previewing the customers collection with a find() query to confirm Alice Smith's existing email. Then run updateOne with $set to change Alice's email to the new address. Next, confirm Charlie Brown's orderCount and run updateOne with $inc to increment it. For Diana, use $push to add a VIP tag to her orders array and then run find() to confirm the new value. To reactivate inactive users, use updateMany with a filter that selects isActive false and a $set to true. Finally, run deleteOne to remove the record for Eve Adams after confirming it exists. After each command, inspect the returned fields such as acknowledged and modifiedCount or deletedCount. screens.title: Operator-based update vs. replacement
screens.narratorSegment: This comparison clarifies the difference between operator-based updates and full replacement. Operator-based updates such as $set and $inc modify specific fields while leaving the rest of the document intact. They are the right choice for incremental changes, analytics counters, or lightly evolving schemas. replaceOne, in contrast, replaces the entire document with the provided document object except for _id which is preserved. Use replaceOne for situations where you have a fully-validated canonical document to swap in, such as after a schema migration that produces a normalized record. A common mistake is accidentally calling updateOne with a plain document (no operators) and unintentionally replacing the document. Another misconception is thinking replaceOne is safer because it's explicit; it's safer only when you intentionally prepared the replacement document and backed up fields you need to keep. Key takeaway: prefer operator updates for partial, safe changes and reserve replaceOne for intentional full-substitution scenarios where no existing fields should be preserved except the identifier. screens.narratorSegment: This slide collects common mistakes and safety patterns you can apply immediately. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, updateOne updates a single matching document and updateMany updates all matches; both accept a filter and an update document that typically uses update operators. Second, the common operators—$set, $inc, $unset, $push, and $pull—let you change values, adjust counters, remove fields, and mutate arrays without replacing the entire document. Third, replaceOne replaces a full document and will remove any fields not present in the replacement; use it only when you intentionally need a full substitution. Finally, always verify operation results by inspecting acknowledged, modifiedCount, or deletedCount and use find() to diagnose unexpected outcomes. These practices protect your data and make updates and deletions predictable and auditable.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a dependable habit for changing and removing data in MongoDB. We cover how to target documents with filters, update fields with operators such as set, increment, unset and array modifiers, and when to use a full replace versus a targeted update. You will also practice safe deletion patterns and how to verify results so you avoid accidental data loss. Throughout we use concrete shell examples and a short customers lab that illustrates common tasks: change an email, bump a counter, add an array tag, revive inactive customers and remove a single record. Why this matters: update and delete operations are destructive when done incorrectly, so learning to verify filters and check operation results is essential to being a responsible DBA. Expect short live-coding demonstrations and reflection prompts that help you decide when a replace is appropriate versus a targeted update. At the end you’ll be able to pick the right method, run it safely, and confirm the change.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to perform targeted updates and deletions with confidence. First, you will use updateOne and updateMany to change single or multiple documents, creating precise filter documents that limit the scope of change. Second, you will apply and combine update operators such as set to change values, inc to increment counters, unset to remove fields, and push or pull to modify arrays. Third, you will recognize when replaceOne is appropriate for a full-document replacement and how it differs from an operator-based update. Finally, you will perform deletion operations with deleteOne and deleteMany while applying safety checks to avoid mass data loss. Each objective includes a short practice task so you can verify the results using the returned counts and acknowledged flags. These skills matter because updates and deletes are destructive when misused; we focus on filters, verification, and safe workflows to keep your data accurate and intact.

This objective slide maps each skill to a small, verifiable task you can run in the MongoDB shell. For updateOne and updateMany, write filters that match precisely and run find with the same filter before you update. For operator practice, perform one command using set to change multiple fields, one using inc to raise a numeric counter, one using unset to remove a field, and one using push followed by pull to add and remove array elements. For replaceOne, construct a full document that intentionally omits a field and explore the effect, verifying that only the _id remained. For deletions, run a find first, then deleteOne for a single record and deleteMany only after confirming the filter. After each command, inspect the returned acknowledged, modifiedCount, or deletedCount values. These simple tasks make verification a habit and reduce the chance of accidental data loss in production.

Let's define the fundamental shape of an update operation. Every update call has two primary parts: a filter document and an update document. The filter is a query that selects which documents will be considered. If you use updateOne, at most a single matching document changes. If you use updateMany, all documents that match that filter are modified. The update document normally uses special update operators such as set or inc; without any update operator MongoDB treats the second argument as a full replacement. A concrete example: to change a product price you build a filter for the product identity and an update document with set to alter the price. A common misconception is assuming updateOne updates one field only — updateOne will apply whatever operators you supply to one matching document, including adding or removing several fields at once. Another pitfall is an overly permissive filter; an empty filter or a filter with broad criteria can update many records unexpectedly. Key takeaway: always design a precise filter and prefer operator-based updates for partial changes. Which fields will you include in your filter next time you update data?

The $set operator is the most common tool for changing values inside a document. It assigns a field to a new value and creates the field when it doesn't exist. Use $set when you need to change single fields like an email or multiple fields such as price and lastUpdated in one command. A concrete example is updating a customer's email: you build a filter that matches the customer's name and a $set update specifying the new email address. A typical misconception is using $set when you actually want to remove a field; for removals use $unset. Another important detail: $set only touches listed fields, leaving everything else intact, which makes it safe for partial updates. After running $set, check the command result for modifiedCount to confirm the change. Practice: preview with find(), then run an updateOne that uses $set to change two fields, and verify modifiedCount equals one. This habit makes partial updates predictable and reversible through controlled changes or backups. $set for single and multiple field updates means $set changes or adds specified fields. combine multiple assignments in one update document to change several fields atomically on the matched document.. In practical terms, set a field value or multiple fields safely with $set. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

$inc and $unset are complementary operators you will use frequently. Use $inc to increment or decrement a numeric field by a specified amount. It creates the field if it doesn't exist and applies the numeric change. For example, incrementing an orderCount by one is a standard operation for tracking activity. One misconception is expecting $inc to create non-numeric fields; if the target field has a non-numeric value the operation will fail. Use $unset when you want to remove a field entirely from a document. The value you supply to $unset is ignored; the presence of the field key in $unset signals removal. A common error is attempting to set a field to null to remove it — null leaves an empty field, while $unset removes the key. In practice, combine these operators where appropriate: increment counters for analytics and unset deprecated fields that no longer serve the document model. After each operation, confirm the modifiedCount to ensure the intended documents changed. $inc and $unset — counters and field removal means $inc changes numeric fields by an amount and $unset removes a field key from matching documents.. In practical terms, increment numeric fields and remove unwanted fields safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Arrays are common in MongoDB documents and the $push and $pull operators let you manage them directly. Use $push to append a value to an array field. If the field does not exist, MongoDB will create an array containing the pushed value. $pull removes all instances of a specified value from an array. A frequent use is adding tags or status markers and later removing specific ones. A misconception is treating $push like a set — it does not prevent duplicates; repeated pushes create repeated elements. To avoid duplicates, you can use $addToSet (not covered in detail here) or check presence before pushing. Think through your application semantics: do you want multiple identical entries or a unique list? Additionally, applying these operators inside updateMany modifies every matching document's arrays; verify with find() first. Example tasks: push a VIP tag into a user's orders array, then pull it out to simulate removing that tag. After each operation, inspect the document to confirm the array content and length. $push and $pull — modifying arrays means $push appends values to arrays, creating the array if absent; $pull removes all matching values from an array.. In practical terms, append and remove values from array fields safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

replaceOne substitutes an entire document for the first match of the filter, preserving only the existing _id value. Because it replaces, not updates, any fields left out of the replacement document will be removed. Use replaceOne when you want to provide a complete, new document shape — for example, a canonical record produced by a migration or a strict replacement after validation. A common misconception is believing replaceOne is just a different name for updateOne; it's not. If you omit update operators in an update call, MongoDB may treat the call as a replacement and replace the document. To avoid accidental replacement, always use operators when you intend partial changes. In practice, before using replaceOne, run a find() to capture the existing document for backup, and be explicit about fields you want to keep. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deleting documents is irreversible in normal operation, so we treat delete commands with high caution. deleteOne removes a single document that matches the filter; deleteMany removes every document that matches. This slide collects common mistakes and safety patterns you can apply immediately. The most frequent errors are forgetting update operators, using an overly broad filter, and not verifying operation results. A missing operator can turn an update call into a replacement, stripping fields you intended to keep. An empty filter passed to deleteMany will delete every document in a collection. Safety patterns: always run find() with the same filter before performing updates and deletes; check the returned result object's modifiedCount or deletedCount; use targeted unique fields in filters when possible; and keep recent backups or snapshots for recovery. For automated scripts, include a dry-run option that logs the matched documents before executing a destructive action. In a critical environment, require peer review of deleteMany operations. Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, updateOne updates a single matching document and updateMany updates all matches; both accept a filter and an update document that typically uses update operators. Second, the common operators—$set, $inc, $unset, $push, and $pull—let you change values, adjust counters, remove fields, and mutate arrays without replacing the entire document. Third, replaceOne replaces a full document and will remove any fields not present in the replacement; use it only when you intentionally need a full substitution. Fourth, deleteOne removes a single matching document while deleteMany removes all matches; preview your filter with find() before deleting and avoid deleteMany with an empty filter. Finally, always verify operation results by inspecting acknowledged, modifiedCount, or deletedCount and use find() to diagnose unexpected outcomes. These practices protect your data and make updates and deletions predictable and auditable.

Conclude with three compact reminders you can use as a checklist. First: always preview with find() using the exact filter you plan to run. Second: use update operators—$set, $inc, $unset, $push, $pull—for partial changes; reserve replaceOne for intentional full replacements. Third: verify operation results by inspecting acknowledged and modifiedCount or deletedCount, and keep backups available for recovery. These three habits—preview, operator-first, verify—will prevent common mistakes such as accidental replacements and mass deletions, and they will make your maintenance operations safe and auditable.
